1:
"Now it came to pass in the days when the judges ruled, that there was a famine in the land." Ellicott renders the phrase literally — when the judges judged — and says at once that the note of time is by no means definite. The witnesses then spend their ingenuity on it and reach no agreement. Gill reports that Josephus placed it under Eli, which is too late for Boaz to be the grandfather of Jesse; that some Jewish writers made Ibzan the same man as Boaz, which is also too late and rests on no proof; and that the Jewish chronology comes nearer the mark in carrying it as high as Eglon king of Moab, when Ehud was judge, with which Lightfoot broadly agrees in placing the story between the third and fourth chapters of the book before it. Clarke lists the candidates without disguising the confusion — Ehud, Gideon, Barak, Abimelech, Shamgar — and notes that Usher settled on the last and that most chronologers followed him. Henry and Ellicott both reason from the genealogy instead, and reach the same answer: it must be early, since Boaz was the son of Rahab, whom Ellicott sees no reasonable ground for supposing to be other than the Rahab of Jericho. Henry adds that the learned bishop Patrick preferred Gideon's day, because only then do we read of a famine caused by an invasion.

Clarke also settles what kind of book this is. It is evidently an appendix to the one before it, containing a perfect history in itself and therefore not to be inserted anywhere within it; it serves as an introduction to what follows, where the history of David is told; and it is not without its use in the Gospels, since it ascertains the line by which Christ came. Henry puts the same thought devotionally: while the judges were ruling, and some one city and some another, Providence takes particular cognizance of Bethlehem, having an eye to a King who should descend from two Gentile mothers. Wesley compresses the whole of it into a sentence — it must be early, for Boaz was born of Rahab, so Christ descended from two Gentile mothers.

The names carry the story before the story begins. Keil and Delitzsch give them as genuine Hebrew: Elimelech, to whom God is King; Naomi, the gracious; Machlon, the weakly; Chilion, pining. He notices that the two Moabitess names resist the same treatment — the sense of turning the back given to Orpah is very arbitrary, and deriving Ruth from a word for a friend is quite uncertain. Clarke and Ellicott render them much alike, sickness and wasting, and Ellicott suggests the names were given by reason of the boys' feeble health and point forward to their early death. Wesley turns it into a proverb: such are the products of our pleasant things, weak and infirm, fading and dying. Gill notes that Elimelech's name suits the age, the government being then a theocracy, and reports the Targum's judgement that he was a great man.
3:
The narrative kills three men in three verses, and the witnesses read the pace as deliberate. Elimelech dies first, and the text leaves Naomi with her two sons. Gill reports Josephus as making Elimelech live ten years in Moab and see his sons married, but prefers Alshech's reading of the text, that the marriages followed the father's death; Clarke agrees that he probably died a short time after his arrival. Gill sets out what the death left behind it plainly enough — she in a strange land without a husband, and they without a father.

The marriages divide the witnesses more than anything else in the chapter. Gill reports Aben Ezra's view that the women were proselytes before the match, and thinks it plainly so of Ruth at least, whether before or after; but he sets against it the Targum's flat verdict that the sons transgressed the decree of the Word of the Lord and took to them strange wives, and observes that some writers excuse the marriage and others condemn it. Clarke simply endorses the Targum as proper. Ellicott reads the act as a second step down from a first: the fault of settling on heathen soil, begun by the father, is carried on by the sons in marrying heathen women, which was to incur a further risk of being drawn into idolatry, as a later and greater king found. Wesley states the alternatives and declines neither — either they were proselytes when they married, or the sons sinned and were punished with short life and want of issue. Gill alone looks past the question to the outcome, that however it was, the thing was so permitted and so ordered in providence that from one of these women the Messiah might spring.

Ellicott adds what can be said about the two names. Ruth will mean either comeliness or companion, according to which spelling the present form is taken to contract, and the Syriac supports the second; she was the wife of Mahlon, apparently the elder son. He notes too that the Targum makes Ruth the daughter of Eglon king of Moab, and sees the motive plainly — an obvious wish to exalt her dignity.

Then the sons die, and the question of judgement becomes explicit. Gill and Clarke both carry the Targum's verdict that because they transgressed the decree of the Word of the Lord and joined in affinity with a strange people their days were cut off; and Clarke, who rarely lets a Targum stand unexamined, adds that it is very likely there is more here than conjecture. Ellicott will not go so far. They died clearly as quite young men, he says, and it is not for us to say how far those are right who see in the deaths of Elimelech and his sons God's punishment for the disregard of his law. What he will say is what the verse says: Naomi is left alone, as one on whom the loss of children and widowhood come suddenly together. Wesley ends on the same two losses and turns them into the question the rest of the chapter answers — by whom shall she be comforted? It is God alone, he says, that is able to comfort those who are thus cast down.
6:
Word reached the country of Moab that the LORD had visited his people in giving them bread, and Naomi arose with her daughters in law to return. Henry makes the verse a portrait of her affection for the land she had left. She could not stay in it while the famine lasted; she would not stay out of it once the famine ceased. Moab had given her shelter and supply in a time of need, but she never meant it for her rest, since no land could be that but the holy land where the sanctuary was. And God, he says, returned at last in mercy to his people: though he contend long he will not contend always, and plenty is his gift. Gill puts her motive more sharply still — she wanted the better opportunities of serving the Lord that her own country afforded, and had no heart to remain in an idolatrous land where she had buried a husband and two sons. Wesley glosses: bread, that is, food; so she stayed no longer there than necessity forced her.

Clarke collects what the Targum adds, that she heard the news by the mouth of an angel, and that the Lord visited his people because of the righteousness of Ibzan the judge and the supplications of pious Boaz; he also records the conjecture that Mahlon and Chilion are the two men named elsewhere as having married in Moab. Gill notes that the text says the country or field of Moab rather than any city — from which some have supposed that the family were either not permitted to dwell in the towns, or chose not to, the better to avoid their neighbours' idolatry.

How far the two younger women meant to go is itself disputed. Gill reads the setting out as an escort only: it does not appear to have been their intention to go with her into Canaan, and he places the parting at the utmost limits of Moab, on the borders of Israel. Ellicott reads it the other way, that both were clearly purposing to go with Naomi to the land of Israel and not merely to see her a little way, since Naomi had won their affections and they were loth to part from her when such a parting could hardly be anything but final. Keil and Delitzsch make the grammar carry the distinction: the word return, taken strictly, applies only to Naomi, who was going back, while her daughters-in-law simply wished to accompany her.

The dismissal is the tenderest thing in the chapter, and each witness notices a different tenderness. Keil and Delitzsch observe that she sends them to their mother's house and not their father's, though Ruth's father was still living, because a mother's love knows best how to comfort a daughter in her affliction. Wesley reaches the same point by custom, that daughters conversed more with their mothers and lived in the same apartments, which were distinct from the men's. Ellicott calls her love wholly unselfish: their company would plainly have been a great solace, and she will not sacrifice them to herself; they each had a mother and a home, and the home was the one thing she could not secure to them. Gill records how the older readers tried to supply the elliptical blessing — the Targum filling it out as a perfect reward, Aben Ezra as a husband, Josephus as happier marriages than they had made with her sons — but thinks none needed, since what follows is the sum of the wish. Ellicott hears it as a twofold blessing made the more solemn by naming the covenant God twice: mercy in general first, and then the particular mercy of rest in a new home. Then she kissed them, and they lifted up their voice and wept.
10:
"And they said unto her, Surely we will return with thee unto thy people." The answer is unanimous, and Naomi spends the next three verses trying to talk them out of it. Gill thinks she suspected their resolution sprang from natural affection only and not from any love to the God or the people of Israel — or at least doubted it, and wished to find out whether either of them was moved by religion at bottom. He adds the pastoral motive: she wanted them to consider thoroughly what they were doing, lest they should afterwards repent and apostatise and so bring a reproach upon the true religion.

Her argument turns on a law they would have known. Wesley points to the ancient custom and the express statute behind her words, which she had doubtless acquainted them with before, along with the other branches of the religion she had brought into the house. Keil and Delitzsch spell out the logic: she is not pregnant with sons who, as younger brothers of Mahlon and Chilion, would carry the obligation of marrying them, so if they go with her there is no hope of their marrying again or enjoying the pleasures of life once more. Clarke lays the address out in its steps and admires it as he goes — she intimates that she has no other sons to give them; that she is not with child, so there is nothing to expect; that she is too old to have a husband; and that even if she married that night and bore sons, they could not wait until such sons were marriageable. Gill notes how far the supposition has to be stretched to be refused at all, since it is not to be thought they would tarry first for the marriage, then for the birth, then for the boys to reach a man's estate.

Ellicott watches the effect rather than the argument. The advice thus far is insufficient to shake the affectionate resolve of the two women, so she turns from their prospects to her own and paints the loneliness of her lot: she has no more sons and can hope for none, and even if sons were born to her now, what good would that do them? Her lot is worse than theirs. They, in spite of their great loss, are young, and may go forth from their mothers' houses to homes of their own; she is old, childless and solitary, and must wend her weary way back to live unaided as best she may.

The last clause of her speech is disputed. The received rendering makes her grief run outward — it grieveth me much for your sakes — and Wesley takes it that way, listing what grieves her: that they are left without the comfort of husbands or children, that she must part with such affectionate daughters, and that her circumstances are too mean to let her invite them, so mean that Ruth would shortly be gleaning for a living. Ellicott judges a different sense much more probable, that it is far more bitter for me than for you, and marshals the evidence — an exact parallel of construction elsewhere, with the Septuagint, the Peshito Syriac and the Targum all supporting it, and only the Vulgate rendering loosely. Wesley, whichever way the clause runs, finds the right posture under it: it is with me that God has a controversy, and such language becomes us when we are afflicted, for though many share the trouble we are to hear the voice of the rod as if it spoke to us alone. And did she not wish to bring them to the worship of the God of Israel? Undoubtedly she did — but she would have them first consider upon what terms, lest having set their hand to the plough they should look back.
14:
They weep a second time, and then the two daughters-in-law part company: Orpah kisses her mother-in-law, and Ruth cleaves to her. Gill reads that second weeping as the sound of women who cannot bear the thought of parting, or that they must be obliged to it. Clarke notes that the Septuagint adds a clause the Hebrew does not have, and returned to her own people, and that the Vulgate, Syrian and Arabic say the same. Wesley takes the kiss for what it is: she departed from her with a kiss and bade her farewell for ever, for she loved Naomi, but not so well as to quit her country for her sake. Ellicott is gentler about the calculation and more exact. Orpah is unwilling to leave her mother-in-law and warmly attached to her, but she thinks of the hardships of the journey and of the hardships waiting when the journey is done, and the comforts of home detain her. Henry and Wesley then turn her into a warning in almost the same words: many have a value for Christ and yet come short of salvation by him, because they cannot find in their hearts to forsake other things for him; they love him and yet leave him, because they do not love him enough, but love other things better.

The last argument is spoken to Ruth alone, after Orpah is gone, and it is Naomi's hardest. The witnesses divide over what she meant by it. Wesley hears a test — she says it to try Ruth's sincerity and constancy, and to intimate that if she came she must embrace the true religion, since those who forsake the communion of saints will certainly break off their communion with God. Gill says the same of the whole speech: this steadfastness was what Naomi wanted to make trial of. Ellicott hears something plainer and less flattering, a fresh argument pressed in earnest, and adds a criticism of the speaker: Naomi views the Moabite gods as realities whose power is merely confined to the land of Moab, and is not sufficiently enlightened in her religion to see in the Lord more than the God of Israel. Clarke settles the religious standing of the two young women bluntly — they were probably both idolaters, Chemosh being the grand idol of that nation, and the conjecture that they had been proselytes is unfounded. Ruth's conversion, he thinks, probably commenced at this moment. Henry, who has just used Orpah as the warning, uses Ruth as the contrary example, of the grace of God inclining the soul to choose the better part.
16:
The reply is the most quoted sentence in the book, and the witnesses attend to its grammar as much as to its beauty. Gill lingers on the first clause, where the verb means something nearer do not meet me or be against me: do not meet her with objections, do not stand in her way, since to be against her going was to be against her inclination, her desires, her resolutions and her interest. Ellicott observes that the intensity of her feeling comes out all the more strongly now that she pleads alone, and that her nobleness is proof against everything Naomi can say. Keil and Delitzsch identify the closing words as a fixed formula used in swearing, by which the speaker calls down a severe punishment upon himself should he fail to keep his word. Ellicott agrees that Ruth clinches her resolution with a solemn oath, and observes that if the words are taken literally she swears by the name of the God of Israel. Clarke says a more perfect surrender of friendly feelings to a friend was never made, and evidently without any secular motive; he also records that she kept it, since Naomi was nourished in the house of Boaz in her old age and became nurse to Obed.

Clarke sets beside the verse the Targum's expansion of it, in which Ruth asks to become a proselyte and Naomi answers with the cost: the Sabbath and its limit of two thousand cubits, the rule against lodging with Gentiles, the hundred and thirteen precepts, the prohibition of strange worship, the four kinds of capital punishment, the house of burial — and to each Ruth returns one clause of her famous speech. It is very likely, he thinks, that some such conversation took place between the elders and those who were becoming proselytes. He adds, and then refuses to elaborate, that the verse is famous among those who strive to divine by the Bible; he saw the practice in his youth and was terrified by it, and will not relate the particulars lest he prolong it.

Wesley and Gill both dwell on the burial clause. She does not desire so much as her dead body carried back into the land of Moab, and having joined souls with Naomi she would have them mingle dust, in hope of rising together. Gill presses it to the same country, the same cottage, the same bed and the same grave, and marks what it costs her: she has no regard at all to the sepulchres of her fathers, which people in all ages and countries have been fond of being laid in. Then Naomi saw she was stedfastly minded, a word Keil and Delitzsch render as stiffening oneself firmly upon a thing, and gave up persuading her any more. Those who are half resolved, says Wesley, are like a door ajar, which invites a thief; resolution shuts and bolts the door, and then the devil flees from us.
19:
The road out of Moab gets one clause of narrative and no incident in it, and Gill fills the silence. He has the two of them keep together and go straight on, without lingering by the way: Ruth was younger and could have walked faster, but she kept company with her ancient mother and was no doubt much edified by her pious conversation. He notices what is not in the scene as much as what is — no camels nor asses to ride on, no servants to assist them, only the two of them on foot, such were their mean circumstances. Ellicott measures the distance and finds it not less than fifty miles, with two rivers, Arnon and Jordan, to be forded or otherwise crossed, and the road for two women apparently alone long, toilsome and not free from danger. He also catches an asymmetry: though news of the end of the famine had reached Naomi in Moab, news of her had not reached Bethlehem. So they arrive weary and travel-stained, and the neighbours, who doubtless never looked to see her again, are all astir.

"Is this Naomi?" Keil and Delitzsch settle who is speaking. The verbs are feminine, so the subject is the inhabitants of the town and chiefly the women of it, who were the most excited at her return; and their amazement is not so much that she was alive as that she came back in so mournful a condition, a solitary widow without either husband or sons. Ellicott agrees on the grammar and adds that grief and toil had made her look aged and worn. Clarke reads the commotion as respect, and argues backward from it that Elimelech must have been of high consideration in the place; Henry argues the same way, that so much notice would not have been taken of her had she not formerly lived respectably, and that a fall out of a high and prosperous condition is always the more remarkable. Henry then allows both tempers in the crowd. Some may have gathered to enquire after her and bid her welcome; some, he grants, may have been moved lest she should prove a charge to the town, for she looked so bare; and if any asked the question in contempt, upbraiding her with her miseries, he calls that temper base and sordid, since nothing is more barbarous than to triumph over the fallen. But he thinks most asked it in commiseration — is this she that lived so plentifully, and kept so good a house, and was so charitable to the poor? — and he reaches for three images to carry the change: the gold become dim, the rose withered and unlike itself blooming, and those who had seen the magnificence of the first temple weeping at the meanness of the second. Wesley puts the same question in one line, asking how marvelously her condition is changed.
20:
Her answer turns on her own name. Clarke glosses Naomi as beautiful or pleasant and Mara as bitter, one whose life is grievous to her. Ellicott calls it one of the constant plays upon words and names found in the Hebrew Bible, notes that her complaint uses the very root of the new name she asks for, and pauses to deny a popular connection: Mara has nothing to do with Miriam or Mary, which come from a different root. Gill cites Josephus for prosperity and grief, then declines to lean on him, since he is not always correct in his interpretation of Hebrew words nor to be depended on; the words mean sweet and bitter. On the title she gives God, Clarke and Ellicott read the same self-sufficiency two ways: for Clarke the All-sufficient has taken away the props and supports of her life; for Ellicott the God who gives all things in abundance is he who takes back.

"I went out full, and the LORD hath brought me home again empty." Wesley fills out the fulness — a husband, sons, and a plentiful estate for their support — and reads the last verb judicially, that God has borne witness as it were in judgment and given sentence against her. Clarke supposes Elimelech carried considerable property into Moab, as a man fleeing a famine would, and that Naomi subsisted on it until it was spent, which may be why she did not think of returning sooner. Gill reports the harsher Jewish reading, that some blamed the family for going abroad at such a time out of a covetous disposition and an unwillingness to relieve the poor who came to them in their distress, and were punished for it; he rejects it as said without any just cause or reason that appears.

The chapter closes on a season rather than a sentence. Gill notes that the summary verse is the writer's own observation, put there to excite the attention of the reader to what follows, against Aben Ezra, who took it of a return at some other time. The witnesses then date the season differently: Clarke puts the beginning of barley harvest in the beginning of spring, immediately after the passover, and adds the Targum's claim that they arrived on the very day the sheaf was first mown to be waved before the Lord, a circumstance he thinks distinctly marked because of the gleaning that follows; Ellicott, calling barley the earliest harvest, puts it about the end of April, and hears in it that the wayfarers arrive to witness and receive their share of the restored plenty. Clarke closes with an argument from manner rather than matter: the amiable simplicity with which the story is told is a proof of its genuineness, for there are sympathetic circumstances here that no forger could have invented, and too much of nature to admit anything of art. Henry makes the plainer point, that they came seasonably, and that our times are in God's hand, both the events and the time of them.
